questions.question: What did the king announce? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The old king of China announced that he was **thinking about choosing a new king for his country** and that he would choose him **from among the common young people of his kingdom**.

**What the passage says.**

> "The Chinese king was old and he was thinking about to chose a new king for his country. He anounced to chose new king from the common people of his country."

**Why it mattered.** Instead of following the custom of choosing one of his own children, the king did "something different": he called all the young people of the kingdom together and set them a test. Every one of them was given a seed and told to bring back what grew from it after a year.

questions.question: What did the king ask the young people to do? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He asked every young person to **take the seed he gave them, plant and sow it, water it and take care of it**, and then **bring the plant back to him after one year**, when he would judge the plants and decide the new king.

**Detail from the passage.** Each youth received "one very special seed", and the king told them he would "see what they had grown from the one seed" and then choose the next king. Ling, the central figure, went home, got a pot and soil from his mother, planted the seed and watered it carefully every day — but nothing ever grew.

questions.question: Why did Ling feel like a failure? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Ling felt like a failure because **around his house all the other young people were talking about the plants they had grown, but there was no sign of development in his own seed** — his pot stayed empty.

**Detail from the passage.** Three weeks, four weeks, five weeks and six months passed and "still nothing" grew. Everyone else had tall plants while Ling had nothing, so he concluded that he had killed his seed. He stopped talking about it to his friends but kept watering the pot and waiting. When the year ended he was ashamed to carry an empty pot, and had to be persuaded by his mother to be honest about what had happened.

questions.question: Why didn't Ling want to go to the palace with his empty pot? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Ling did not want to go because **he was afraid of the laughing of people and of his failure at having an ungrown seed**; he wanted to stay at home rather than carry an empty pot before the king.

**Detail from the passage.** He told his mother that he was not going to take an empty pot, and when he did reach the palace "he felt sick to his stomach". Seeing the beautiful plants of the other youths, he put his empty pot on the floor and "many of the others laughed at him", which is exactly what he had feared.

questions.question: How did the king praise Ling? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The king told the whole crowd that **Ling alone had the courage and honesty to bring the pot with the original seed in it**, and declared, "Behold your new king! His name is Ling!"

**Detail from the passage.** When the king spotted Ling at the back with his empty pot he had him brought to the front; Ling was terrified and thought he would be killed for his failure. Instead the king explained that **the seeds had all been boiled and could never grow** — everyone else had cheated by planting another seed, and only Ling had been truthful.

questions.question: Find the words from the passage which mean the same as: (i) very frightened (8th para) (ii) bravery (last para).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) very frightened — **terrified**; (ii) bravery — **courage**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "Ling was **terrified**. He thought that the king was angry. May be he would have Ling killed because of his failure!"

> "Ling was the only one with the **courage** and honesty to bring me a pot with my seed in it."

Both words fit the sense of the paragraph but the exam asks for the exact single word the passage uses, so write only "terrified" and "courage" in the answer sheet.

questions.question: Read the passage on greenhouse gases and find at least eight important points in it; use them as sub-headings to make notes and give a suitable title.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: The Greenhouse Effect and Our Duty**

1. **Carbon dioxide — the main greenhouse gas**
   (a) animals give it out when they breathe
   (b) plants absorb it
   (c) amount of CO₂ stays the same in nature

2. **Modern lifestyle**
   (a) upsetting the balance
   (b) burning fuels in vehicles & power stations

3. **Burning of tropical rain forests**
   (a) land cleared for development
   (b) releasing CO₂, fewer plants left to absorb it
   (c) a double problem

4. **Methane**
   (a) a greenhouse gas
   (b) released by animal waste, swamps, rice fields, oil & gas rigs

5. **Nitrous oxide**
   (a) comes from car exhausts
   (b) from chemical fertilizers

6. **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)**
   (a) used in refrigerators, aerosols, foam packaging
   (b) small in quantity but 10,000 times more effective at trapping heat

7. **Slowing the greenhouse effect**
   (a) produce less of the gases that cause it
   (b) governments already reducing CFC use
   (c) reduce use of fossil fuels — petrol, oil, natural gas, coal

8. **Our duty**
   (a) learn to use energy sources that do not burn and release CO₂
   (b) choose alternative sources — wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric

**Key to abbreviations.** CO₂ – carbon dioxide; CFC – chlorofluorocarbon; chem. – chemical; alt. – alternative; atmos. – atmosphere.

questions.question: Write a summary of the greenhouse-gas passage in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas, and in nature plants and animals keep its amount in balance. Modern life disturbs this balance: vehicles and power stations burn fossil fuels, and tropical forests are burnt for development, releasing carbon dioxide while leaving fewer plants to absorb it. Methane, nitrous oxide and chlorofluorocarbons add to the problem, CFCs being 10,000 times more effective at trapping heat. The only way to slow the greenhouse effect is to cut these gases and use alternative sources such as wind, solar and tidal energy.

**Word count.** About 90 words. The examination accepts 75–90; keep to the passage's own order of ideas.

questions.question: You lost your mobile phone in the school/college campus. Write a notice for the notice board in about 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. P. COLLEGE, NOTICE BOARD**

**NOTICE**

*Date: 10 March 2015*

**LOST MOBILE PHONE**

A mobile phone, a **Micromax A069 of green colour**, has been lost somewhere in the college premises. Whoever finds it is requested to bring it to the owner, **Rahul Kumar of Class XII A**. The founder will be duly rewarded with a party.

**Rahul Kumar**
Class XII A
Mob. No.: 9211420143

**Format points.** Word "NOTICE" at the top, the name of the institution, the date, a boxed body, and the writer's name and class at the bottom left; keep to 50 words and do not add a salutation or a subscription.

questions.question: The Principal of your school/college has invited you to be a member of the cultural committee. Write a note accepting the offer in about 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Akash Kumar**
Lalpur, Ranchi
27 February 2015

The Principal
St. Albert School
Ranchi

**Subject: Acceptance of membership of cultural committee**

Sir

Your invitation to the membership of the cultural committee is a very honourable proposal for me. I am obliged to accept this invitation and I will try my best whatever I can do for this committee.

**Akash Kumar**

**Format points.** A formal note of acceptance carries the writer's address and date, the addressee, a subject line, a short body that **accepts expressly**, and the writer's name — all within 50 words.

questions.question: You went to see a film in a modern multiplex for the first time. Describe your experience of the event in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Last Saturday I went to watch a movie at **Eylex Cinema Hall**, and it was the first time I had entered a modern multiplex. From the outside the building looked like a glass palace; inside, the lobby was all polished tiles, coloured lights and the smell of popcorn.

The ticket counter was a row of computer screens, and we were handed printed tickets in seconds. The hall itself was a grand one with a **huge screen and rows of soft, reclining seats**. There was a big crowd, but the air-conditioning kept everything cool and quiet.

When the lights dimmed the screen filled with colour and sound so real that I forgot I was sitting in a hall. During the interval we bought snacks and cold drinks and came back to our seats. Munching popcorn while watching a film on that vast screen was a new pleasure altogether. I came home thinking it was a memorable moment for me.

questions.question: There was a Blood Donation Camp in your school/college. Write a report of the event to be published in the school/college magazine in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**BLOOD DONATION CAMP HELD IN COLLEGE**

*By a Staff Reporter*

**Dhanbad, 20 September 2015.** A blood donation camp was organised in the assembly hall of **J. P. Inter College, Dhanbad**, on Saturday in association with the District Blood Bank. The camp was inaugurated by the Principal, who donated blood himself and urged the students not to be afraid of the needle.

A team of doctors and technicians from the civil hospital examined every donor before collection. More than **two hundred students and teachers** came forward, of whom one hundred and forty were found fit to donate. Each donor was given a certificate, fruit juice and a packet of biscuits. The collected blood was taken to the blood bank in a refrigerated van.

The secretary of the students' council said the camp would be held twice a year. The Principal thanked the doctors and declared that the college would keep serving the district in this way.

questions.question: The mobile phone that you lost is with the Principal of your school/college. Write an application asking the Principal to give you your mobile phone in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Rakesh Shah**
Class XII A
St. Paul Sr. Secondary School
Hazaribagh
30 March 2015

The Principal
St. Paul Sr. Secondary School
Hazaribagh

**Subject: Request for taking back the mobile phone**

Sir

I am a student of class XII. I have lost my mobile phone because of using it in the class. I came to know that the phone has been deposited with you.

I request you to return my mobile phone because it is a very necessary means of communication and I am residing outside of my hometown, so it becomes more necessary for me. I assure you that I will not bring the phone to the classroom again and will keep it switched off during school hours. I will ever be grateful to you for this kind act.

Yours obedient pupil
**Rakesh Shah**
Class XII A

**Format points.** Sender's address with the date, the addressee, a subject line, the salutation "Sir", a body that states the facts and then the request, and a formal subscription — all in about 125 words.

questions.question: You feel that all politicians cheat us with promises which they never fulfil. Write a letter to the Editor of *The Statesman* expressing your disappointment in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**12, Circular Road**
**Ranchi**
**14 April 2015**

The Editor
*The Statesman*
Kolkata

**Subject: Disappointment at politicians' unfulfilled promises**

Sir

Through your esteemed daily I wish to express my deep disappointment at the way our politicians treat the voter. Every election brings the same long list of promises — roads, water, electricity, jobs, a school in every village — and every election is followed by the same silence.

The candidates who visit our mohallas during the campaign are not to be seen again for five years. When a genuine grievance is taken to them, we are told that the matter is "under process". It is not the promise that hurts so much as the calculated deception behind it.

I would request the public to judge leaders by what they have already done rather than by what they say they will do.

Yours faithfully
**Amod Kumar**

**Format points.** Statement of the problem, evidence or consequence, and a remedy; restrained tone — a letter to the editor argues, it does not abuse.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Swachh Bharat Abhiyan' for your school magazine.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**SWACHH BHARAT ABHIYAN**
*— Clean India, Healthy India*

Hon'ble Prime Minister of India Sri **Narendra Modi** introduced a nationwide social campaign keeping in mind the dreams of the Father of the Nation, **Mahatma Gandhi**, of keeping clean the country. On **2 October 2014**, the Prime Minister organised a ceremony and introduced 'Swachh Bharat Abhiyan' towards the nation. He requested all the people to keep clean their houses and surroundings.

The campaign is not a programme of the government alone. Its success depends on the habit of every citizen — using dustbins, keeping drains covered, refusing polythene, and treating public places as one's own courtyard. In villages, toilets and proper waste pits have changed the lives of women especially. In cities, cleanliness must be coupled with a system that collects garbage daily instead of piling it at the corner of the street.

Our school can begin with a simple rule: every class clears its own room and one hour every Saturday is given to the campus. If each one of us cleans one small patch, the whole country will be clean.

**Format points.** A title, the writer's name or designation below it, short paragraphs, and a balanced view — an article describes, explains and persuades.

questions.question: India has made a steady progress with its space programme. Write an essay on the 'Mangalyaan Space Project' in 150–200 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THE MANGALYAAN SPACE PROJECT**

On **24 September 2014** India placed a spacecraft in orbit around Mars and joined a very small club of space-faring nations. The mission, named **Mangalyaan** (Mars Orbiter Mission) and built by ISRO, was launched from Sriharikota on 5 November 2013 by the PSLV C-25 rocket.

What makes the project remarkable is that it succeeded **at the very first attempt**. The craft had to travel about 670 million kilometres, leaving the earth's orbit, surviving the long solar journey and then being slowed at exactly the right moment so that the gravity of Mars would capture it. ISRO's engineers called that final manoeuvre "the most difficult part", and it worked to the second.

The most striking feature of Mangalyaan was its **economy**: the whole mission cost less than a big Hollywood film, roughly seventy-four million dollars. Its instruments study the atmosphere and the surface of Mars, looking especially for methane, which may indicate life in the past.

Mangalyaan has become a symbol of Indian scientific self-reliance. It has proved that a developing country can do world-class space research with modest resources and great skill, and it has encouraged a whole generation of students to look at the sky.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet from which this extract has been taken: 'Fisherman in the harm cold sea / Would not harm whales / and the man gathering salt / Would look at his hurt hands.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Keeping Quiet**; poet — **Pablo Neruda**.

**Context.** These lines come in the middle of the poem, where the poet imagines the stillness of the count-to-twelve moment working its way into ordinary labour. The fisherman would stop his work in the cold sea and **not harm the whales**, and the salt-gatherer would pause and **look at his own hurt hands** — that is, for once he would notice the injury his trade has done him. The idea is that a short, deliberate silence gives each person time to see what his own activity costs him and others.

questions.question: What would the fishermen do when everything is quiet? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The **fishermen would not harm the whales**. Their activity in "the harm cold sea" would pause, and in that silence they would spare the creatures they usually kill.

**Context.** Pablo Neruda's poem imagines a moment when everyone together counts to twelve and stays silent. In that hush "he would not harm the whales", the man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands, and those preparing for war would wear clean clothes and look at their own hands. The lines suggest that a little quietness can turn human energy from hurting to seeing.

questions.question: What would the salt gathering man do in the quietness of the moment? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The salt-gathering man "**would look at his hurt hands**". In the stillness his hands would become an object of attention — and with them the bitter price his trade has been exacting from his own body.

**Explanation.** His hands are sore and cracked with salt and water, yet in the rush of work he never notices them. The silent moment would make him pause and "look at his hurt hands", which is also the poem's way of asking all of us to look honestly at the injury our livelihood does to us.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Aunt Jennifer's Tigers prance across the screen. / Bright topaz denizens of a world of green. / They do not fear the men beneath the tree; / They pace in sleek chivalric certainty.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Aunt Jennifer's Tigers**; poet — **Adrienne Rich**.

**Context.** These are the opening lines of the poem. Aunt Jennifer is embroidering tigers that "prance" across the panel of cloth; they are "bright topaz denizens of a world of green" and they move "in sleek chivalric certainty". The tigers stand for everything the embroiderer is not — fearless, confident and free — while the woman who creates them sits in her chair with a heavy wedding ring weighing down her hand.

questions.question: What were Aunt Jennifer's tigers doing? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** They were **prancing across the screen of her embroidery**, bright yellow (topaz) inhabitants of a world of green, pacing in "sleek chivalric certainty" and **not afraid of the men** sitting beneath the tree.

**Explanation.** The tigers exist only in the cloth, but rich uses them as a contrast to their creator: they are bold where she is "mastered by" her husband's will, they are free of fear where she is "terrified". They are the courage she cannot express in her own life.

questions.question: Where are the men in the extract? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer: **Answer.** The men are **beneath the tree** in the tigers' green world. The tigers "do not fear the men beneath the tree" — the uncle who may be inside that house has no power over them.

questions.question: What did Sarojini Naidu feel sad when she saw her mother? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The speaker of the poem (Kamala Das) feels sad when she sees her mother because **her mother has grown old and is suffering, and the daughter can do nothing about it**. Seeing her mother's face "ashen like that of a corpse", she is filled with the old childhood fear of losing her.

**Explanation.** The poem is spoken by a daughter sitting beside her mother on a journey to the airport. Looking at the "pale as a late winter's moon" face of the old woman, she realises how age has reduced her mother to weakness and dependence. She pushes the thought away by looking out at the "young trees" and "merry children", then hides her fear behind a smile and says, "see you soon, amma".

**Note on the printed booklet.** It attributes the feeling to "Sarojini Naidu"; the poem *My Mother at Sixty-Six* is by **Kamala Das**. The printed sense of the answer — a daughter's grief at her mother's ageing — is what the examiner wants.

questions.question: What do the poor children in the slum classroom look like? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The school children of slums represent a **very pathetic picture**. They have **pale and lifeless faces**. Their **disorderly hair are torn around and look like rootless wild plants**.

**Explanation.** From Stephen Spender's "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus): one boy is "like a paperweight", another "short, strange, pale", others stand with "slagged" heads and "hair around their faces like rootless weeds". The images insist that these children are starved of air, sunlight and hope, and that the classroom's map on the wall does not connect with their lives.

questions.question: Pablo Neruda wants us to keep quiet for some time. Why? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Pablo Neruda wants us to keep silence for some time because **a huge silence can do us a lot of good when we are disappointed at not understanding ourselves or threatening ourselves with the death**.

**Explanation.** Counting to twelve and staying still would break the "sadness of never understanding ourselves" and stop the rush in which "we are preparing for war". It would let fishermen spare the whale, the salt-gatherer look at his hurt hands, and men in uniform look at their own hands instead of their weapons. The silence is not the silence of death but of a new understanding — "it should be counted as twelve and stay quiet".

questions.question: Why do the rural people make roadside stands? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rural people make roadside stands for their survival. They think that urban people will come there and will buy some useful home articles and will pay some money.

**Explanation.** In Frost's poem the "roadside stand" is a small hut with "wild berries" and "squash" set out for city cars. The stand is a hope: the villagers believe the passing traffic will stop and pay for their produce, and that with the money they can have "some city money to feel in hand". Frost's irony is that the cars "halt" only to ask about the distance to the next town.

questions.question: How was M. Hamel dressed for school that day? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** M. Hamel had put on his **fine Sunday clothes**: his **beautiful green coat**, **frilled shirt** and the **little black silk cap, all embroidered**.

**Explanation.** In "The Last Lesson" Franz notices this unusual dress before anything else, and it frightens him: the teacher normally wears a loose work jacket with a ruler under his arm. The Sunday dress is a sign that the day is a special one — the last French lesson before the German masters take over the school — and later M. Hamel wears the same stillness as he announces, "we have not given up".

questions.question: Who was Saheb? What did he do to earn some money? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Saheb was a **neighbour of the author** and he was a **ragpicker**. He had come from **Bangladesh**. He earned money by **working at a tea-stall** after first being a ragpicker.

**Explanation.** In "Lost Spring" Saheb is the barefoot young boy of Seemapuri who begins as a ragpicker, going barefoot through heaps of garbage in search of a rupee or a coin. Later he takes a job at a tea-stall for eight hundred rupees and all his meals — a job that pleases the author less than it pleases him, because it costs him his freedom.

questions.question: Who was Rajkumar Shukla? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rajkumar Shukla was a **poor peasant**. He was from **Champaran**. He was a **sharecropper, illiterate**, and came to Gandhi to **complain about the injustice being done by the landlords of Champaran**.

**Explanation.** In "Indigo" Shukla is "resolute" and follows Gandhi everywhere, from the Congress session to his ashram, until Gandhi agrees to go to Champaran. He is the living evidence that the Champaran sharecroppers were bound by an unfair agreement with English landlords, and he becomes a volunteer in the campaign.

questions.question: How did the old crofter earn 30 kroners? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The crofter's **cow (bossy) was extraordinary**. She gave milk for the **creamery everyday**. Last month he had received **thirty kroner in payment**.

**Explanation.** In "The Rattrap" the old man who gives the peddler shelter is a former crofter who lives alone. He shows off the three ten-kroner notes which the creamery paid him for milk and hides them in a leather pouch under a stone; the peddler watches where they go and steals them the next morning, which is the crime that starts the story's moral test.

questions.question: Why was the rattrap peddler afraid to walk on the highway? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He had **stolen thirty kroners of the crofter**, so he was thinking about his wealth. He did not dare to go through the public highway **bewaring of being caught**.

**Explanation.** Selma Lagerlöf's peddler has taken the old crofter's money, so he leaves the road and enters the forest to avoid the police and the people who might recognise a "peddler with a pack". The forest too becomes a trap, with its "moss-covered stones" and paths that turn in circles, until he reaches the Ramsjö iron works.

questions.question: Who were Jansie and Sophie? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophi and Jansie are **classmates and friends**. They belong to **poor families**. Sophie is very ambitious, on the other hand Jansie is a **practical girl** who accepts reality.

**Explanation.** In A. R. Barton's "Going Places" both girls have finished school and will work in the biscuit factory. Jansie urges Sophie to be "sensible", while Sophie builds fantasies about Danny Casey, the football player, and about a boutique of her own. Their talk about "the shops" and the "loads of money" shows the narrow choices of their world.

questions.question: How did the British officials treat Gandhiji at Motihari and Champaran? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The behaviour of the British officials was **very rude and unjustified** towards Gandhiji. He met the secretary of the British landlord's association, but he did not give him any information. Gandhi met the commissioner who only **bullied him and advised him to leave the place**. Gandhiji did not leave.

He proceeded to Motihari, the capital of Champaran. A peasant had been maltreated in a nearby village, and Gandhiji went there on the back of an elephant. He was asked to return to the town. He was served with an **official notice to quit Champaran immediately**. He made it clear that he would **disobey the order**, and he received a summons to appear in court the next day.

The court appearance became his strength: thousands of peasants gathered outside the courthouse, the officials felt powerless, and the case against him was dropped. Gandhi then accepted a compromise settlement giving the sharecroppers their money back and, more importantly, the confidence that they had rights.

**What the episode shows.** In "Indigo" the clash is between an official order and a moral claim; the British could summon and serve notices, but once the peasants stood together the officials could not govern without consent.

questions.question: Why was Douglas afraid of water? What happened to him as a child? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** William Douglas was afraid of water because of **an accident in his childhood**. When he was three or four years old, he went to a beach in California with his father. A big wave knocked him down and **buried him in the water**. He was terrified, and the experience left a lifelong fear of water in him.

The fear grew worse when he was ten or eleven. He was learning to swim at the Y.M.C.A. pool at Yakima when a big boy threw him into the deep end. He went down, struck the bottom, came up with his lungs full and sank again. He was "paralysed" with fear and almost drowned before he reached the side by himself.

**How he conquered it.** Douglas later hired an instructor who taught him to exhale, kick and float, and he practised for months in the pool, in Lake Wentworth and finally in the warm ocean at Baja California. The fear had been real but, as he writes, "the will to live grew in me". He learned that water is not an enemy but a force to be understood.

questions.question: Why and how did Dr. Sadao help the prisoner of war to escape? Do you find him guilty of harbouring an enemy? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dr. Sadao had given a **new lease of life to the American prisoner of war**. He and his wife Hana took a lot of pains to save his life. He did not want to throw him into the jaws of death again. He asked the young soldier to take his **private boat at night**. He should row in the cover of darkness to a **little island nearby**. The island was deserted, so nobody lived on it. The young American could live there until he saw a **Korean fishing boat pass by**. Many of them passed near the island. He put **food, bottled water and two quilts** in the boat. If the food ran out, he could signal two flashes; he was not to signal in darkness because he could be seen. The American came down into the darkness of the garden and escaped. The prisoner had gone **quite safe**.

**Guilt?** No, Dr. Sadao cannot be found guilty of harbouring an enemy. No doubt the nations of countries at war are considered enemies, but we should not forget that Sadao was a **doctor**, and for a doctor **saving a dying man is the foremost priority**. It doesn't matter if the dying man is an enemy.

**Deeper point.** Sadao's decision costs him his peace of mind — he is an enemy in Japanese eyes and a traitor to his training if he hands the man over. The story shows a doctor's humanity winning over his patriotism, though he never quite stops being afraid of the consequences.

questions.question: Who was Annam? What did he say to little Bama? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** In "Memories of Childhood" Annam is the **elder brother of Bama**, the little Tamil girl who tells the story. He is a college-going boy in a village near Madras and he is the one who makes her understand the meaning of the humiliation she sees on the street.

Bama once saw an old man of her own community carrying a small packet of *vadai* by its string, without touching it, because he was a "lower caste" man and the upper-caste shopkeeper would not let him touch anything. She told Annam about it, and he explained that this was **untouchability** — that the man was not allowed to touch the packet because of his caste.

Annam told her that **education was the only way out**. If she studied hard and did well, she could **make her own way in the world** and would not have to bend before such customs. He said that the community had been kept ignorant for centuries and that learning was the weapon with which they could break the chain.

**Result.** His words made Bama study with new determination; she stood first in her class, and her story ends with the hope that the small events of childhood can change a whole life.

questions.question: What did the astrologer predict when the Tiger King was born? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** When the Tiger King was born, the astrologers predicted that **his death would come from a tiger**.

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story the chief astrologer reads the stars over the infant prince and warns that the child will one day have to meet his death from a tiger. The Maharaja grows up determined to defeat the prophecy by killing every tiger in his kingdom, which is precisely how the prophecy comes true — the hundredth tiger is a wooden toy bought for his son, and a sliver of it kills him.

questions.question: What types of story did Jack usually tell his daughter? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Jack usually told stories of **small creatures**. Every story had a **small creature usually named Roger**. It could be **Roger fish, Roger Squirrel or Roger chimpunk**. In every story Roger went to the wise owl.

**Explanation.** In "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus) Jack tells his four-year-old Jo a story every Saturday evening. The formula is fixed: a small animal with a problem goes to the wizard, gets changed, and then the wise old owl sends him back to be changed again. Jo, however, has begun to ask awkward questions about the ending.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: What was Gondwana? What happened to it? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Gondwana was a **giant southern supercontinent**. It existed about **six hundred and fifty million years ago**, centred around present-day **Antarctica**. After thriving for 500 million years it was **forced to separate due to geological phenomena** and broke into separate countries as they exist today.

**Explanation.** In Tishani Doshi's "Journey to the End of the Earth" Gondwana explains why Antarctica matters: its climate was much warmer, it had a huge variety of flora and fauna, and humans had not appeared. Its break-up created the continents and the oceans that now shape the world's climate, which is why the ice-core records of Antarctica are read as the earth's memory.

questions.question: Why does Mr. Lamb have a tin leg? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Mr. Lamb has a **tin leg** because **one of his legs was blown off in the war**. He became a **physically disabled person** and walks on an **artificial tin leg**. But he does not feel like a handicapped person or suffer from an inferiority complex.

**Explanation.** In Susan Hill's play Mr. Lamb tells Derry that he lost his leg in the war and now wears a tin one. Children call him "Lamey-Lamb", and he simply lets the name pass. His lameness is the reason he can understand Derry, whose face was burnt by acid, and it is his cheerful acceptance that makes him able to say, "it's all relative".

questions.question: Who was Zitkala Sa? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Zitkala Sa was a **Native American woman** (a Sioux) who writes the first half of "Memories of Childhood". As a child she was taken from her mother and sent to a **white man's school**, where her long hair was cut and she was made to feel "an enemy of the whites".

**Explanation.** Her account describes the "cutting of my long hair" as the moment of her worst humiliation, because in her tribe shingled hair was worn only by mourners and cowards. She hid under a bed, was dragged out and tied to a chair, and the scissors were used on her. Her story shows how schooling was used to erase a child's culture.
